## Overview and grading

### What you'll practice

This graded assignment has two parts:

- In **Part I**, you'll run a multi-step RNA-seq workflow on the @garrigós2025 data,
  from raw reads to transcript counts.
  You'll organize it like we discussed in week 10:
  with single-step shell scripts that you submit as Slurm batch jobs,
  and a Markdown "protocol" with the code to run these scripts in order.
  Along the way, you'll quantify gene expression with Salmon,
  and you'll summarize the results of all steps in a single MultiQC report.

- In **Part II**, you'll install Positron on your own computer and connect it to OSC.
  You'll use Positron to write and run R code in the remaining weeks of the course,
  starting with the week 12 class on Monday, November 9^th^.

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday Nov 8^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**: Like for GA3 and GA4,
  you will submit your assignment by tagging the instructors in an Issue
  in your GitHub repository, as per the last step below.

::: callout-note

for one of GA3, GA4, or GA5.

## Part I: A multi-step workflow

### General

- **Two Markdown files**:
  - Like before, we provide a **template** `README.md` with a section for each question,
    where you add your answers (see "Setting up" below).
    Add commands and their output only where the template asks for them.
  - Separately, you'll build the **protocol** for your workflow in a file `protocol.md`,
    which should contain the final code to run all steps in order,
    like the [protocol example in w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#a-protocol-example).
    You don't need to repeat this code in your `README.md`.

- For **each step** where you run a shell script one or more times, you should:
  1. Submit the shell script as one or more batch jobs
  2. Monitor the progress of the job(s)
  3. When they are done, check the Slurm log files and the output files
  4. If you detect failures, try to figure out what went wrong, and rerun
  5. Move the Slurm log files of the successful run(s) into a `logs` dir within
     the script's output dir^[
     The scripts create these `logs` dirs for you.
     This is a small addition that you haven't seen in scripts so far.]

- **Commit** your files to your Git repo as you go along,
  using informative commit messages: commit at least once per Part (A--E).

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
The workflow is similar to
[the protocol example in w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#a-protocol-example),
but not identical!
To get some genuine practice,
and to avoid copying the wrong things,
we recommend not to copy-paste code from that lecture page.
:::

### Setting up

- Start a VS Code session at OSC OnDemand as per usual,
  and open a terminal in that session.

- Create a new dir for this assignment, `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/GA5`.
  Then, open this dir as your VS Code folder with `File` > `Open Folder`.
  *This will be your working dir for the entire assignment.*

- Copy the **template file** for this assignment,
  `/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA5/GA5_template.md`,
  into your working dir as `README.md`.

- Create a file `protocol.md` in your working dir,
  and copy the following protocol template into it:

  ````{.markdown .file filename="protocol.md"}
  # RNA-seq analysis of _Culex pipiens_

  - Author: <???>
  - Date: <???>
  - GitHub repository: <???>
  - This was run at the <???> cluster of the Ohio Supercomputer Center (<www.osc.edu>)
  - OSC working dir: <???>

  # Base output dir:

  ## Step 1: Read QC with FastQC

  The `fastqc.sh` script runs on 1 FASTQ file at a time and takes 2 arguments:
  the input FASTQ file and the output dir.

  ```

  ## Step 2: Read trimming with TrimGalore

  <???>

  ## Step 3: Creating a transcriptome index with Salmon

  ## Step 4: Pseudo-alignment and quantification with Salmon
  ````

### Part B: Read QC and trimming

05. Using the code in your protocol, run the FastQC script for all FASTQ files.
    (You'll have to fill in one blank in the loop.)
    How many batch jobs did you submit, and did they all succeed?

06. Take a look at the `trimgalore.sh` script,
    which is similar to the one you worked on in GA4,
    paying particular attention to the arguments it takes.
    Then, add a loop to your protocol that runs the script once per sample,
    and run it.

    ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
    #### The TrimGalore output files _(Click to expand)_
    Unlike the TrimGalore script from GA4,
    this script renames the trimmed FASTQ files to the same names as the input files,
    like `S63_R1.fastq.gz`.
    Since TrimGalore runs FastQC on the trimmed files _before_ this renaming,
    the FastQC output files still have names like `S63_R1_val_1_fastqc.html`.
    :::

07. With 22 samples, you won't want to open every Slurm log file to check
    whether its job succeeded.
    Since the scripts print a line `# Successfully finished script <script-name>`
    at the very end,
    write a command that **lists the TrimGalore Slurm log files that do _not_ contain
    this line**.
    (If all jobs succeeded, this command should print nothing:
    to make sure your command works, you can test it on a file that you know
    doesn't contain the line.)

08. The TrimGalore script reserves 8 cores for each job.
    Use the `seff` command,
    explained on the [self-study Slurm page](../bonus/slurm.qmd#seff-resource-usage-of-a-finished-job),
    to check the resource usage of one of your TrimGalore jobs
    (you can find the job ID in the Slurm log file name).
    What were the CPU efficiency and the memory usage?
    Based on this, would you change the number of cores for this script?

### Part C: Transcript quantification with Salmon

In week 11, the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline first aligned the reads
to the reference **genome** with STAR,
and then used Salmon to quantify gene expression based on those alignments.
Here, you'll use Salmon on its own:
it can also directly map the reads to the reference **transcriptome**,
i.e. to the sequences of all annotated transcripts,
and estimate how many reads came from each transcript.

This approach is often called **pseudo-alignment**^[
Salmon's documentation calls its default mode "selective alignment",
while "pseudo-alignment" is the term introduced by the similar program kallisto.
In practice, "pseudo-alignment" is commonly used for both,
including by the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline, which can run Salmon in this way
with its `--pseudo_aligner salmon` option.],
because it doesn't produce full read alignments.
Compared to aligning to the genome, it has the following advantages and disadvantages:

- Pseudo-alignment is **much faster** and needs much less memory.
- It doesn't need to be "splice-aware" like STAR:
  since transcript sequences don't contain introns,
  reads from mature mRNAs match them without gaps.
- But you **can only quantify known transcripts**,
  i.e. those in the annotation,
  and you don't get alignment (BAM) files,
  which you would need for other purposes,
  like visualizing alignments or calling variants.

Like with most aligners, Salmon needs an **index** of the reference sequences.
You'll first create this index, once,
and then quantify each sample against it.

09. Neither of the Salmon scripts contains a container link yet:
    the line `SALMON_CONTAINER=<???>` near the top is incomplete.
    Get a link from the Seqera Containers website to a container
    with the most recent version of Salmon,
    and add it to both scripts.
    Then, test the link by printing Salmon's version with this container,
    and commit the updated scripts.

10. Take a look at the `salmon_index.sh` script,
    and figure out how you should run it.
    Then, add the code to do so to your protocol, and run it.
    (Only a single index is needed, so you'll run this script just once.)
    When it's done, report how long it took to create the index,
    and how large the index dir is.

11. Now, you can quantify the trimmed reads against the index.
    The script `salmon_quant.sh` does this for _one sample_ at a time,
    and takes 4 arguments:

    1. An R1 FASTQ file
    2. The matching R2 FASTQ file
    3. The Salmon index **dir**
    4. The output dir (the script will create a subdir for each sample in there)

    Read the script, add code to your protocol to run it for all samples, and run it.

    <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Which FASTQ files should you use as input? _(Click to expand)_</summary>

    You should use the _trimmed_ FASTQ files produced by TrimGalore,
    not the raw FASTQ files.
    Therefore, your loop should not loop over the files in `$fastq_dir`.

    </details>

12. Take a look at the main output file for sample `S63`,
    `quant.sf`, and use the [Salmon documentation on its output files](https://salmon.readthedocs.io/en/latest/file_formats.html){target="_blank"}
    to answer the following:
    - What do the `TPM` and `NumReads` columns contain?
    - This file has counts for transcripts, not genes.
      But for most analyses, such as a differential expression analysis,
      you'll want counts per gene.
      What extra information would you need to get from transcript counts to gene counts?

13. Salmon reports the **mapping rate**,
    i.e. the percentage of reads that it could assign to a transcript,
    in the file `logs/salmon_quant.log` within each sample's output dir.
    Write a command that prints the mapping rate for all samples at once.
    Which sample has the lowest mapping rate?

14. The `salmon_quant.sh` script uses `--libType A`,
    which makes Salmon automatically detect the library type
    (e.g. whether the library is _stranded_, as you may recall from week 1).
    In the output files for sample `S63`, find the library type that Salmon inferred.
    Then, use the [Salmon documentation on library types](https://salmon.readthedocs.io/en/latest/library_type.html){target="_blank"}
    to explain what this library type means.

### Part D: Summarizing all steps with MultiQC

In GA3, you ran MultiQC on FastQC output only.
But MultiQC recognizes the output of hundreds of bioinformatics programs,
including TrimGalore and Salmon,
and it can summarize all of these in a single report ---
like the report that you saw for the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline in week 11.
So here, you'll run MultiQC once, at the end of the workflow,
on your entire `results` dir.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
MultiQC only recognizes the output of TrimGalore version 2 (which we're using)
since MultiQC version **1.35**.
If your GA3 script used an older version, update its container link.
:::

15. Your `multiqc.sh` script from GA3 was written to be run directly with `bash`.
    Update it so that it is also suitable to be submitted as a batch job,
    following the other scripts for this assignment.
    That is, it should:
    - Have `#SBATCH` lines with the OSC project,
      a descriptive Slurm log file name, and email notification for failed jobs
    - Print the logging statements that the other scripts print
    - Create a `logs` dir in the output dir

    Then, commit the updated script.
    Since the script is in your Git repo,
    `git diff` (before committing) or the Git log will show exactly what you changed.

16. Add code to your protocol to run MultiQC with `results` as the input dir,
    and `results/multiqc` as the output dir, and run it.
    In the Slurm log, MultiQC reports the number of reports it found for each program.
    For each program, explain why it found this number of reports.

    <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Rerunning MultiQC? _(Click to expand)_</summary>

    As you saw in GA3, when MultiQC finds an existing report in its output dir,
    it adds a suffix to the names of its new output files,
    unless you use its `--force` option.
    So if you need to rerun MultiQC, you can first remove the old output files.

    </details>

17. Download the MultiQC report (`results/multiqc/multiqc_report.html`),
    open it in your browser, and answer the following:
    - In the **General Statistics** table at the top,
      which sample has the lowest Salmon mapping rate,
      and does this match your answer to question 13?
    - The FastQC section includes the results for both the raw and the trimmed reads.
      Pick one FastQC metric that differs between raw and trimmed reads,
      and describe the difference.
    - In week 11, you downloaded the MultiQC report of the nf-core _rnaseq_ run
      on the same data
      (`week11/results/nfc-rnaseq/multiqc/star_salmon/multiqc_report.html`).
      In that report, find the percentage of reads that STAR aligned
      to the genome for a few samples.
      How does it compare to your Salmon mapping rates for those samples,
      and what could explain the difference?

## Part II: Positron setup {#part-ii-positron-setup}

### Part E: Install Positron and connect to OSC

In the remaining R weeks of the course,
you'll write and run R code in **Positron**,
an IDE (Integrated Development Environment) created by Posit,
the company behind the popular R IDE RStudio.
Positron is a newer alternative to RStudio,
and a great fit for this course:

1. It is **built on VS Code**^[
   Specifically, on Code OSS, the open-source base of VS Code.
   Positron is really a variant ("fork") of VS Code.],
   so it will look and feel very familiar:
   the Command Palette, the Explorer, the terminal, extensions, and settings
   all work just like in VS Code.
2. On top of that, it adds **data science features** that VS Code lacks,
   like an R console, and panes for your variables, plots, and help.
3. Positron, not RStudio, is the main focus of Posit's development moving forward.
4. It has much better support than RStudio for Python and for AI assistance.

Unlike VS Code Server, Positron is not available through OSC OnDemand.
Instead, you will **install Positron on your own computer**,
and **connect it to OSC** using SSH.
This means that like with VS Code Server,
your files, R, and your R code will all be at OSC:
only the program's interface runs on your computer.

::: callout-important
#### If you get stuck
If you can't install Positron, or can't get the connection to OSC to work,
email us well before the deadline, and we'll help you.
If we can't solve it before the deadline either,
you can still earn full points for questions 18 and 19:
describe what you tried and where you got stuck,
and do question 19 with RStudio Server at OSC instead,
as explained in the [last section of this page](#fallback-rstudio-server-at-osc).
:::

#### Install Positron

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
#### If you have an OSU-managed computer without admin rights _(Click to expand)_

You should still be able to install Positron,
but do so at the **user level rather than system-wide**:

- On a **Mac**, drag the Positron app into your **personal** Applications folder,
  `/Users/<username>/Applications`
  (this folder is in the same parent folder as your Documents, Downloads,
  and Desktop folders).

- On **Windows**, the Positron installer has a **user install** option:
  look for a checkbox or dropdown labeled "Install for me only"
  (vs. "for all users") during setup.
:::

1. Go to the [Positron download page](https://positron.posit.co/download.html){target="_blank"}
   and check the box to accept the license agreement.

2. Download the latest release for your operating system:
   - **Mac**: Look for the `.dmg` file (Intel or Apple Silicon)
   - **Windows**: Look for the `.exe` installer
   - **Linux**: Look for the `.deb` or `.rpm` file, depending on your distribution

3. Install Positron:
   - **Mac**: Open the `.dmg` file and drag Positron to your Applications folder.
   - **Windows**: Run the `.exe` installer and follow the prompts.
   - **Linux**: Use your package manager to install the downloaded file.

4. Open the program!

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Installing R on your own computer _(Click to expand)_
You don't need R on your own computer for this course,
because you'll be using R at OSC.
But if you want to use Positron for R work outside of OSC,
you'll need to install R separately, since Positron does not come with its own R:

- **Windows**: use [this `.exe` file](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/release.htm)
- **Mac**: use [this `.pkg` file](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/R-latest.pkg)
- **OSU-managed computer**: use the Software Center (Windows)
  or Ohio State Application Self Service (Mac)
:::

#### Set up the SSH connection

Because Positron is built on VS Code,
it connects to OSC in the same way as a local VS Code installation does,
using the same SSH configuration.
That setup is described on the
[page on connecting a local VS Code installation to OSC](../bonus/vscode-local.qmd),
and you can **follow it in Positron** instead of in VS Code:
it is identical, except that you don't need to install any extension,
because Positron has remote SSH support built in.

Specifically, in Positron,
follow these sections of that page:

- [The SSH configuration file](../bonus/vscode-local.qmd#the-ssh-configuration-file)
- [Avoid being prompted for your OSC password](../bonus/vscode-local.qmd#avoid-being-prompted-for-your-osc-password)
- [The proxy script at OSC](../bonus/vscode-local.qmd#the-proxy-script-at-osc)

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
If you already did this setup for a local VS Code installation,
you can skip the above steps:
the SSH configuration lives in a file on your computer (`~/.ssh/config`),
which Positron will use as well.
:::

Then, **increase the connection timeout**:
because it can take a little while to get a compute job,
open the Positron **Settings** ({{< fa cog >}} > `Settings`),
search for `remoteSSH.connectTimeout`,
and change its value from 15 to **300** (seconds).
(Note that the name of this setting is slightly different than in VS Code.)

#### Connect to OSC from Positron

1. Open the **Command Palette**
   (<kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>P</kbd> or `View` > `Command Palette`)
   and type "_**SSH connect**_".

2. Select `Remote-SSH: Connect to Host...` and then choose `osc-pitzer-compute`:

   ![](../img/vscode-select-connection.png){fig-align="center" width="50%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the list of SSH hosts to connect to."}

3. A new Positron window will open and connect to OSC.
   This may take 30 seconds or more while a compute node is being allocated.

   - If you're asked about the operating system of the host, select **Linux**.
   - If you're asked whether you "trust the authors", click **Trust and Continue**.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
#### If the compute node connection fails or takes more than a few minutes _(Click to expand)_
See [this box](../bonus/vscode-local.qmd#connecting) on the local VS Code page.
:::

18. Once connected, open a **terminal** in Positron (`Terminal` > `New Terminal`).
    This works just like the VS Code terminal, and it's running at OSC.
    In this terminal, run the `hostname` command, and report its output.
    Based on this output, are you on a login node or on a compute node?
    Also report which version of Positron you installed
    (you can find this under `Help` > `About`,
    or on a Mac, under `Positron` > `About Positron`).

#### Load R at OSC {#load-r-at-osc}

R is installed but not automatically loaded at OSC.
The easiest way to make sure that Positron will find R when it connects to OSC
is by adding the R module to your Bash settings file, `~/.bashrc`
(recall [week 7's shell configuration material](../bonus/shell-config.qmd)):

1. In your Positron terminal, add a `module load` command for R to your `~/.bashrc` file:

   ```bash
   echo 'module load gcc/12.3.0 R/4.5.2' >> ~/.bashrc
   ```

2. Reload Positron:
   open the **Command Palette**
   and start typing "_Reload Window_", then select "**Developer: Reload Window**".

::: callout-warning
#### This isn't a permanent solution to load R at OSC
Adding this `module load` command to your `~/.bashrc` is not a permanent solution,
because over time, the R versions available at OSC will change,
as may the version that you personally want to use.
On the plus side, this command currently works on all three OSC clusters,
since they have the same R modules.
:::

#### Open your personal folder

Positron really wants you to **open a folder**,
just like VS Code (and in the week 12 lecture, you'll learn why that is a good idea).
Open your personal dir, `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>`
(where `<user>` is your OSC username),
by clicking the "Open Folder" button in the Explorer
or using `File` > `Open Folder`:

![](../img/positron-open-folder.png){fig-align="center" width="50%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Positron Explorer view showing the Open Folder button."}

If you're asked whether you trust the authors of the files in this folder,
click **Yes, I trust the authors**.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Reconnecting from now on
Like in VS Code, after connecting once,
the folder will appear in Positron's "Recent" list on the Welcome tab,
so you can reconnect to OSC _and_ open this folder with a single click.
:::

#### Check that R works

At the bottom of the Positron window, there should be a **Console** tab,
which should have started an R session.
The R version is also shown at the top right of the Positron window,
in the so-called interpreter picker:

![The interpreter picker. You should see R 4.5.2 instead of the version shown here.](../img/positron-interpreter.png){fig-align="center" width="35%" fig-alt="Screenshot of the Positron interpreter picker"}

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
#### If you're seeing a Python console, or no console at all _(Click to expand)_

- If no R or Python version is shown in the top-right corner of the Positron window,
  click on the interpreter picker there.
  If Python is shown instead, it will look like this,
  and you should also click on it:

  ![](../img/positron-python-active.png){fig-align="center" width="40%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Positron interpreter picker showing a Python interpreter."}

- Then, select **New Console Session**:

  ![](../img/positron-new-console-session.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the interpreter picker menu with the New Console Session option."}

- Select R 4.5.2:

  ![](../img/positron-switch-to-r-console.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the list of R and Python interpreters to choose from."}

- When done, you should see this in the top-right instead,
  and your console should have switched to R as well:

  ![](../img/positron-switched-to-r-console.png){fig-align="center" width="40%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the interpreter picker showing an R interpreter."}

If R 4.5.2 isn't listed at all,
check that you completed the [Load R at OSC](#load-r-at-osc) step,
including the window reload.
:::

19. Click in the Console, type the following, and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>:

    ```r
    R.version.string
    ```

    This should print `"R version 4.5.2 (...)"`:
    report the output in your `README.md`.
    Then, take a **screenshot** of your Positron window
    that shows the R console with this output,
    and the Explorer with your personal dir opened.
    Upload the screenshot into a dir `doc` in your `GA5` dir^[
    For example, by dragging and dropping the file from your computer
    into Positron's Explorer, or with FileZilla, as shown in w11c.],
    so that the image shows up in your `README.md` (see the template),
    and commit it.

If this all worked, you're all set for the week 12 class! 🎉

#### Optional: Posit Assistant {#optional-posit-assistant}

<!---- TODO: Decide whether to keep this section here, or move it later ---->

_This section is optional and not graded._

Posit Assistant is Positron's built-in AI coding assistant,
designed specifically for data analysis.
Similar to Claude Code, it can run code for you,
but unlike Claude Code, it can directly see your R session,
including the objects in your environment.

You can use it with the same OSU LiteLLM API key that you used for
Claude Code in [week 9](../week09/w9a_claude.qmd),
and/or with GitHub Copilot.

<details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Set up and test Posit Assistant _(Click to expand)_</summary>

##### Install the Posit Assistant extension

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

1. Open the **Extensions** view by clicking the Extensions icon in
   the Activity Bar (the narrow, leftmost sidebar).

2. In the search box, start typing "**posit assistant**".

3. Click **Install** (when connected to OSC: **Install in SSH: osc-pitzer-compute**)
   on the "**Posit Assistant**" extension by Posit.

:::

::: {.column width="54%"}

![The Extensions icon](../img/positron-extension-icon.png){fig-align="center" width="20%" .lightbox fig-alt="The Extensions icon."}

![](../img/positron-extension-posit-assistant.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Positron Extensions view showing the Posit Assistant extension."}

:::

:::

##### Authentication via the OSU LiteLLM API

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}

1. Click on the newly added **Posit Assistant icon** in the Activity Bar.

2. It should show the following:
   click "Help me set it up" and then "Configure LLM providers".

:::
::: {.column width="30%"}

![The Posit Assistant icon](../img/positron-assistant-icon.png){fig-align="center" width="30%" .lightbox fig-alt="Posit Assistant icon in the Activity Bar"}

:::
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../img/positron-assist-init-setup1.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Posit Assistant panel with the Help me set it up button."}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](../img/positron-assist-init-setup2.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Posit Assistant panel with the Configure LLM providers button."}
:::
:::

3. At the top, select **Custom Provider** from the list of providers, and enter:

   - **API Key**: Use the API key from your `~/.claude/settings.json` file at OSC
     (you can open it in Positron with `File` > `Open File`).
   - **Base URL**: `https://litellm.cloud.osu.edu`
   - Then, click **Sign in**.

   ![](../img/positron-assist-init-setup3.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Custom Provider configuration form."}

4. If it worked, the assistant panel should now show:

   ![](../img/positron-assist-init-setup4.png){fig-align="center" width="40%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Posit Assistant panel after a successful sign-in."}

5. In the bottom-right of the prompt box, click Select Model:

   ![](../img/positron-assist-init-setup5.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Posit Assistant prompt box with the Select Model button."}

6. The models you can access via the API key are available under
   "**OpenAI Compatible**" (the first option in the list):
   click "More models".

   ![](../img/positron-assist-init-setup6.png){fig-align="center" width="35%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the model selection menu."}

7. In the (long!) dropdown list, select a Claude model like `claude-opus-4-6`.
   Then, the prompt should look something like this:

   ![](../img/positron-select-model2.png){fig-align="center" width="75%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Posit Assistant prompt box with a model selected."}

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Model compatibility
Not all models available through the OSU LiteLLM service may work with
Posit Assistant's Custom Provider.
If you get an "**internal error**" when trying to use the Posit Assistant,
switch to a different model and try again.
:::

##### Authentication via GitHub

This is not required if you set up the API key above.
However, like in VS Code, GitHub Copilot will provide inline code completions^[
In Positron, it does so via Posit Assistant rather than via its own extension.],
which access via the API key does not.

1. Click the cog wheel {{< fa cog >}} icon at the top of the Posit Assistant
   panel and select **Configure LLM providers**^[
   This window can also be opened via the Command Palette by typing "_**Configure**_":
   it's listed as "**Configure Language Model providers**".].

2. Select the provider "GitHub Copilot" and click "**Sign in**"
   (keep the default selection of `OAuth` for **Authentication**):

   ![](../img/positron-github-login.png){fig-align="center" width="55%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the GitHub Copilot provider configuration."}

3. A browser window will open, asking you to authorize Posit Assistant to access your GitHub account.
   Log in and authorize as requested.

4. Done! Now, when clicking on the model selection indicator in the Posit Assistant prompt,
   you should see models listed under a GitHub Copilot section header:

   ![](../img/positron-select-model1.png){fig-align="center" width="27%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the model selection menu with GitHub Copilot models."}

##### Testing Posit Assistant

1. In the R console, create a simple data frame:

   ```r
   df <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = rnorm(10))
   ```

2. In the Posit Assistant panel, try asking:

   > Create a scatter plot of x vs y from df

3. Posit Assistant should generate code for a plot and ask for permission to run it:
   click **Allow**.

   ![](../img/positron-prompt1a.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Posit Assistant panel showing a prompt and generated code for a scatter plot."}

4. It produces the plot and shows it in its own panel,
   along with suggestions for next steps.
   The plot should also appear in Positron's Plots pane,
   since it was generated with R code in your R session.

   ![](../img/positron-prompt1b.png){fig-align="center" width="80%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the Posit Assistant panel showing the resulting scatter plot."}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Claude Code in Positron _(Click to expand)_
The Claude Code extension works in Positron just like in VS Code.
Install the "**Claude Code for VS Code**"^[
Yes, "for VS Code", not "for Positron".]
extension by Anthropic in the Extensions view,
and it will use the `~/.claude/settings.json` file at OSC
that you created in [week 9](../week09/w9a_claude.qmd).

Unlike Posit Assistant, however, Claude Code can't see your R session by default.
:::

#### Fallback: RStudio Server at OSC {#fallback-rstudio-server-at-osc}

If you can't get Positron to work,
you can instead use RStudio Server, an Interactive App at OSC OnDemand.
RStudio has the same main components as Positron,
like a code editor, an R console, and panes for your environment, plots, and help,
but they are laid out differently and you'll have to find your own way at times.

1. Log in to OSC's OnDemand portal at <https://ondemand.osc.edu>.
2. In the blue top bar, select **`Interactive Apps`** and then near the bottom,
   click **`RStudio Server`**.
3. Fill out the form as follows:
   - Cluster: **`pitzer`**
   - R version: **`4.5.2`**
   - Project: **`PAS3493`**
   - Number of hours: **`2`**
   - Node type: **`any`**
   - Number of cores: **`1`**
4. Click **`Launch`**.
5. Click the **`Connect to RStudio Server`** button once it appears.

Instead of opening a folder like in Positron,
use an "RStudio Project" for your personal dir:
`File` > `New Project` > `Existing Directory`,
and then browse to `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>`.

## Submission: Publish your repo on GitHub

Finally, you'll publish your Git repo on GitHub and submit your assignment
by creating an Issue.

20. Make sure you have committed your final `README.md` and `protocol.md`.
    Then, create a new, empty, public repository on **GitHub**
    (e.g., named "GA5" or "PLNTPTH5006-GA5"),
    connect it to your local repo, and push your local repo to GitHub.
    (Add the repo's URL to your protocol, commit, and push again.)

    On the GitHub page for your repo, create a new **Issue**.
    Use whatever title you like, and in the text box (not the title),
    tag the instructors: GitHub users `kstarr791` and `jelmerp`
    (using the `@` notation like `@kstarr791`),
    asking them to take a look at your assignment.
